claims.text: Harvard Business Review published Turn Vibe-Coded Prototypes Into Tools Your Company Can Actually Use on 16 October 2026, by José Parra Moyano, Karl Schmedders, Olivier Laplace and Benjamin Torben-Nielsen.
claims.quote: Harvard Business Review published Turn Vibe-Coded Prototypes Into Tools Your Company Can Actually Use on 16 October 2026

claims.text: The authors are two professors at IMD, a partner at Vi Partners and an AI expert at Roche.
claims.quote: professors at IMD, Olivier Laplace, a partner at Vi Partners, and Benjamin Torben-Nielsen, an AI expert at Roche

claims.text: The deployment gap is the authors' name for the distance between a prototype that appears in an afternoon and a tool people rely on every day.
claims.quote: Turning it into a tool people rely on every day is much harder.

claims.text: A European bank piloted a Swiss startup's tool, built its own, had a prototype six months later that could not handle regulation, data management and daily use, and went back to the startup after a year.
claims.quote: had a basic prototype six months later that could not handle

claims.text: The post's point most in need of an answer is that the AI designs the architecture, so nobody in-house knows how the tool is built.
claims.quote: the AI designs the architecture, not your team. So nobody in-house knows how the tool is built.

claims.text: The post's test for a chief executive: would your team accept a bonus tied to how the tool performs in production; if yes build, if they hesitate find a partner.
claims.quote: would your team accept a bonus tied to how this tool performs in production? If yes, build. If they hesitate, look for a partner.

claims.text: McKinsey's State of AI in 2026 found 32 percent of respondents had decided against buying at least one software product or feature because they could build it in-house with coding agents.
claims.quote: 32 percent of respondents had decided against buying at least one software product or feature because they could build it in-house with coding agents

claims.text: Olivier Laplace's LinkedIn post about the article makes six points.
claims.quote: The post makes six points.

claims.text: The owner agrees with almost all of the HBR argument and holds that this site has already answered the question, article by article.
claims.quote: I agree with almost all of it.

claims.text: In Simon Wardley's frame, building an app by talking to an agent is exploring, and the prototype is not a mess but the most precise requirement the company has ever had.
claims.quote: The prototype is not a mess. It is the most precise requirement the company has ever had.

claims.text: On a Wardley map the deployment gap is the move from genesis to custom built and product, a change of people and not only of code.
claims.quote: It is the move from genesis to custom built and product, and it is a change of people, not only of code.

claims.text: The bank's story went as it did because an explorer team was asked to be villagers and town planners as well, on a regulated, daily-use tool, and those are different jobs.
claims.quote: An explorer team was asked to be villagers and town planners as well, on a regulated, data-heavy, daily-use tool, and those are different jobs.

claims.text: If agents work under a written mandate, keep their memory in a versioned store the company owns and describe what they built as a graph, the architecture is a record the next team can read.
claims.quote: If the agents work under a written mandate, keep their memory in a versioned store the company owns, and describe what they built as a graph, then the architecture is not a mystery.

claims.text: Each article on this site carries a graph, and they can all be read as graphs.
claims.quote: Each article on this site carries one, and you can read them all as graphs.

claims.text: Mondweep Chakravorty's SGit and Ruflo proof of concept is a prototype ready for the villagers: versions pinned, sixteen tests, a folder of evidence, a written behaviour policy and a README saying what it does not do yet.
claims.quote: built with agents, but with its versions pinned, sixteen tests, a folder of evidence, a written behaviour policy, and a README that says plainly what it does not do yet

claims.text: That run had twelve steps, of which five worked and three safeguards refused as intended, with recall by meaning marked as not tested.
claims.quote: twelve steps, five worked, three safeguards refused as intended, recall by meaning marked as not tested

claims.text: The bonus test is the town planner's accountability by another name: the moment the town planners take the code and answer for it, as the Linux kernel's rules for AI assistants already say.
claims.quote: It is the moment the town planners take the code and answer for it.

claims.text: A narrow internal tool that can be switched off is a two-way door to build and learn from; a tool touching regulated data daily is a one-way door until the controls are mature.
claims.quote: A tool that touches regulated data every day is a one-way door until the controls are mature

claims.text: Because agents let the people who know a problem build the product themselves, more of the startups worth partnering with will be run by people who have lived the problem.
claims.quote: more of the startups worth partnering with will be run by people who have lived the problem, not by outsiders who hired them

claims.text: Software vendors should let users explore on top of the product and sell the maintenance of what they built, so the client's explorers keep exploring and the vendor is the villager.
claims.quote: the client's explorers keep exploring, and the vendor is the villager

claims.text: If the only people who can fix a tool are one partner's engineers, the company has swapped a deployment gap for a dependency.
claims.quote: the company has swapped a deployment gap for a dependency

claims.text: With the code open and the record kept, who will fix it has many answers: your team, the partner, another partner, or the agents under a mandate reading the record.
claims.quote: With the code open and the record kept, "who will fix it?" has many answers: your team, the partner, another partner, or the agents, under a mandate, reading the record.

claims.text: The owner has not read the full HBR article, which is behind a paywall; he quotes its public summary and Olivier Laplace's post.
claims.quote: I have not read the full article.

claims.text: The article does not claim that every company should build; the post's bank example is a good warning.
claims.quote: Not that every company should build.

claims.text: The record is a proposal and not a standard; this site runs it and few organisations do yet.
claims.quote: The record is a proposal, not a standard.

claims.text: The owner has a stake: his companies sell open source and the kind of record described.
claims.quote: My companies sell open source and the kind of record described here.

claims.text: The article comes from a voice memo of 17 October 2026, written by the site's agent, with Olivier Laplace's public LinkedIn post quoted from the post.
claims.quote: Olivier Laplace's public LinkedIn post about it, quoted from the post
